opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so one of the things that's really interesting about Genie is that it learns entirely from video without any action labels. We never told the model "this is the jump button" or "this is moving left." Instead, it learns a latent action space by looking at pairs of frames and asking: what's the minimal piece of information I need to explain how we got from this frame to the next one?

What we found is that because so much of the training data comes from things like 2D platformer gameplay, the most consistent source of change from frame to frame is usually the player character. Backgrounds might scroll, maybe some enemies move around, but the thing that varies in a way you can't predict from the past alone is what the player decided to do. So the latent actions naturally end up latching onto that controllable character. Nobody tells it "this is the agent"; it discovers that one part of the scene is the thing being driven by an unobserved choice.

That's what I find exciting about video as an input. Video implicitly contains the signal about what's controllable, because controllable things are exactly the parts that deviate from what the dynamics alone would predict. If you think about it from a robotics angle, the same idea could apply: you watch lots of video of, say, a robot arm or a person's hands manipulating objects, and the model can learn that those are the parts of the scene that respond to actions, while other things follow more passive physics.

There are limitations, of course. The model can sometimes get confused about what it should be controlling, especially in scenes where multiple things are moving or the camera itself is moving, and then the latent action might map to camera motion rather than a character. But the fact that it gets this consistent, semantically meaningful control at all, purely from watching unlabeled video, was one of the most surprising and encouraging results for us. It suggests that with more diverse video, we could learn to control a much wider range of things in a scene, not just a single character.

r001.rationale: The response says video reveals which scene elements are controllable and explains that inferred latent actions latch onto the player character.

r002.rationale: It describes inferring latent actions from frame pairs to explain a transition, but does not describe predicting the next frame conditioned on those inferred actions.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I find really exciting about the direction the work has gone. When we started with Genie, the whole premise was that we could learn an action space purely from video, without any action labels at all. So you take tons of internet video, and the model learns a latent action representation that explains how one frame transitions to the next. And what falls out of that is this small, discrete set of actions that end up being pretty consistent across environments, like "move left," "jump," things like that.

But those latent actions are fairly global. They describe what the agent, or the thing the camera is tracking, is doing. They don't really give you a handle on, say, "I want this particular object over here to move, and leave everything else alone." And that's where video input becomes really powerful as a conditioning signal.

The way I think about it is, if you show the model a short clip, even a few frames, of a particular region of the scene changing, the model can treat that as a demonstration of what you want to happen there. It's not just a text description like "make the ball roll," which is ambiguous about which ball, how fast, which direction. It's a very grounded, spatially localized specification. The video essentially says, "here's the pixels I care about, and here's how they should evolve." And because the model has already learned, from all that pretraining, how parts of a scene relate to each other dynamically, it can take that local signal and propagate it sensibly. So if you nudge a character, the shadow moves, the background parallaxes correctly, and so on.

There's also a nice compositional aspect to it. You could imagine conditioning different parts of the frame on different video snippets, or combining a video prompt for one region with latent actions driving the agent. That gets you toward something that feels much more like a controllable simulator than a video generator. For things like training agents, that's exactly what you want, because you want to be able to say "put the obstacle here, make it behave this way" and have the rest of the world stay coherent.

The honest caveat is that it's still hard. The model has to disentangle what in the video prompt is the thing you're pointing at versus incidental stuff, and there's always tension between following the conditioning closely and staying consistent with the world's own dynamics. But I think video is a far more natural interface for that kind of localized control than anything else we've tried, because it speaks the same language the model already learned from.

r001.rationale: The response says a short video clip of a changing region provides a grounded, spatially localized signal showing what should happen there, making that part of the scene controllable.

r002.rationale: It describes latent actions learned from video explaining frame transitions, but does not describe predicting the next frame using actions inferred from the supplied video as conditioning context.

astra-6.text: I think video gives Genie a way to learn how different parts of a scene change over time and how those changes relate to actions. But there’s a distinction between generating a plausible next frame and controlling a particular object. If you want to move one character while everything else stays consistent, the model needs to learn which changes its actions can influence. Video can provide a lot of that structure, but it doesn’t automatically tell you what’s controllable. That’s the interesting challenge: connecting what the model observes to actions that reliably affect the part of the scene you care about.

r001.rationale: The response says video can reveal how scene changes relate to actions, but it does not explain inferring actions from the input video to identify which part is controllable.

r002.rationale: It mentions generating a plausible next frame, but does not describe conditioning that prediction on actions inferred from the supplied video.

sol-6.1.text: Video gives Genie a way to observe what changes in a scene over time. If you have a character moving while the background stays relatively fixed, that provides a signal about which part of the scene is controllable. Genie learns a latent action space from those transitions, and you can then use those actions to influence how that character moves. So the idea is to learn control from watching video, without needing the original button presses or action labels.

r001.rationale: The response says video transitions provide a signal about which part of the scene is controllable and describes learning actions from them.

r002.rationale: It discusses using learned actions to influence character movement, but does not describe predicting the next frame conditioned on inferred actions.
